subject: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
Hi,  I'd like to construct a distribution for a likelihood that differentially weights each likelihood contribution; for example, suppose I'd like to sample:

for( i in 1:N)
  target +=  weight[i] * bernoulli_logit_lpmf(y[i]|alpha)


Either directly updating target or writing a user-defined function that leverages bernoulli_logit_lpmf() for each observation reduces the computational efficiency compared with the vectorized version.   I pulled the rstan package tarball to see if I could find the underlying c++ code for bernoulli_logit_lpmf to directly update it there in order to preserve efficiency and ability to use a vectorized specification under differential weighting.  I could not, however, find it.  Would you offer any recommendations on the best way to accomplish this by-observation weighting of the likelihood in stan?

thanks,

terrance.


--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
On Friday, September 30, 2016 at 10:23:14 AM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
Would you offer any recommendations on the best way to accomplish this by-observation weighting of the likelihood in stan?

I would recommend that you not weight the likelihood when doing MCMC, unless the weights correspond to the number of actually observed observations of that value of y, in which case you should just use binomial_logit_lpmf(). The bernoulli_logit_log() function is defined at

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/prim/scal/prob/bernoulli_logit_log.hpp

although that doesn't help you much because it uses all kinds of internal functions.

Ben

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
the weights are used as a plug-in device to create a noisy approximation for the population likelihood estimated from an informative sample (where the inclusion probabilities for units in the population are correlated with the response variable of interest).   the weights are normalized to sum to the number of (asymptotic) observations in order that the posterior uncertainty is correct.  so the weighting serves to re-balance information in the sample to approximate the balance in the population (and does not represent the number of units in the population).  while there are other fully bayesian approaches, there is a good reason i choose to use this weighted plug-in approach.  the weights can be regressed on the response to reduce their variability if that is problem in estimation.  the approach generally works well in gibbs sampling, though perhaps there would be additional issues in HMC regarding the stability of the sampler geometry.

anyway, thanks for providing me a link to the function.  i see the computation of -log1p(exp(theta)) portion of logp and its gradient, but can't find the n*theta piece, so i don't see a direct way of multiplying by the weights.   i'm guessing that if i write a weighted bernoulli_logit_lpmf() as a user function  that operates on each observation, it will be computationally too slow.  if you have any thoughts here, I'd appreciate having them.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
On Friday, September 30, 2016 at 12:21:34 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
the weights are used as a plug-in device to create a noisy approximation for the population likelihood estimated from an informative sample (where the inclusion probabilities for units in the population are correlated with the response variable of interest).   the weights are normalized to sum to the number of (asymptotic) observations in order that the posterior uncertainty is correct.  so the weighting serves to re-balance information in the sample to approximate the balance in the population (and does not represent the number of units in the population).  while there are other fully bayesian approaches, there is a good reason i choose to use this weighted plug-in approach.

It does not make sense to say the posterior uncertainty is correct for a non-fully Bayesian approach. A fully Bayesian approach yields the posterior distribution conditional on the data in hand, not conditional on what you think / estimate the data are in some larger population. We have had good success with post-stratification approaches.

Ben

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
so there are two distributions that govern the observed sample under a complex sampling design:  1. the population generating distribution; 2. the known sampling design distribution.   the attached paper shows that the plug-in (weighted - based on first order inclusion probabilities) pseudo posterior estimator is frequentist consistent with respect to this joint distribution.

https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ejs/1468847267

even if observations are conditionally independent under the population generating distribution, they are typically not under the sampling design distribution (for samples taken from the population).  if the observations were independent, the amount of posterior information would be the sample size, n.   the theory in the above paper defines a class of sampling designs that guarantee consistency.  the pairwise dependence is required to asymptotically attenuate to 0 for designs in this class - so, asymptotically, the number of observations reflects the posterior uncertainty.   of course, we don't work in asymptopia and an area of active research is approximating the amount of information in the sample where dependence is induced by the sampling design distribution.

all to say, the virtue in the plug-in approach is that it is fully general and offers asymptotically correct inference under any population generating model based solely on observed quantities - the sample observations and weights - with no requirement to know (to parameterize) the sampling design.  

i am familiar with the your approach of using weights to form post-strata.  very clever, but it requires an "information sufficiency" argument - that is, the sample reflects all the information in the population, if in different balance - to avoid imputing the non-sampled units (for consistent estimation).  the paper is not explicit in this point, but it is a requirement.  i hope to use it and, perhaps, further generalize it, but it is a less general approach than the plug-in estimator.  lastly, something not discussed in our preference for fully bayes is whether the data are able to offer any comment on a model for the weights, since the former (data) are acquired under the population generating model and the latter (weights) are acquired under the sampling design distribution.

anyway, if you have any other comments regarding how to implement a weighted likelihood approach that would efficiently sample, i'd appreciate having them.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] building an efficiently sampled weighted pdf/pmf
parts:
Just write the formula out diretly in Stan.

real weighted_bernoulli_logit(int[] y, vector weight, real alpha) {
real succ;
real fail;
succ = 0;
fail = 0;
for (i in 1:N) {
if (y[i]) succ = succ + weight[i];
else fail = fail + weight[i];
}
return succ * bernoulli_logit_lpmf(1 | alpha);
+ fail * bernoulli_logit_lpmf(0 | alpha);
}

And then I'd write:

target += weighted_bernoulli_logit(y, weight, alpha);

I wouldn't write it out using sampling notation as it's
not properly generative and so the notation may be confusing.

Presumably you can compute succ and fail in transformed data
and make the whole thing very efficient.

- Bob

There's a discussion of calculating sufficient
statistics like this in the code optimization chapter
of the manual.

> > I wouldn't write it out using sampling notation as it's not properly generative and so the notation may be confusing.
>
> the resulting joint pseudo posterior is not a proper distribution, so i see your point. the approach does admit proper full conditionals in the case of gibbs sampling.

Can you write out the joint density? If so, there might be a way to
just code that directly in Stan.

It's possible to write down two conditional distributions that aren't
derived from the same joint distribution, but I'm pretty sure that violates
the assumptions built into Gibbs sampling.

- Bob
